1.pericope_label: A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger... The lips of the wise disperse knowledge: but the heart of the foolish doeth not so

schools.summary: Delitzsch works the vocabulary throughout — two distinct words for anger in the first verse, an idiom of mastery in the second, a verb of observing and holding fast in the third, and a noun meaning store rather than force in the sixth — and rejects a rendering that would make the perverse tongue merely violent rather than perverse; Ellicott glosses the proverbs briefly and reads the divine watching as two different waits, one until an iniquity is full and one for a chance to help.
Gill supplies the illustrations, high winds laid by soft showers and a tribe pacified by a mild reply, and insists that a wise tongue is measured by its fitness to its hearers.

Clarke states the mechanism of quarrels, one angry word begetting another as the temper of one spirit reproduces itself in another, sets out at length the difficulty of knowing when and what and how to speak, and divides the omnipresent eye into a thought that appals the guilty and a thought that encourages the upright; Wesley makes the wise use of knowledge a matter of timing and manner, and has the fool pour out folly as a fountain does water.

Henry adds the counter-case to the soft answer, the same tribe exasperated by a rougher man, and gives the group its two best sentences: that hard arguments do best with soft words, and that angels are full of eyes but God is all eye.

debates.question: Whose spirit does a perverse tongue break?

positions.view: Another's; the perverseness is a distortion of truth that deeply wounds the hearer.
Both; the speaker is wounded in his own conscience while the hearer is left with guilt or grief.
The fault is perversity rather than violence, the opposite of truthfulness and kindness, and the wound is to the spirit as such.

debates.question: Is the omnipresent eye a threat or a comfort?

positions.view: Both, and separately: the eye everywhere appals a man who wants privacy for his wickedness, while the providence everywhere encourages the upright in distress.
Chiefly a doctrine of providence, under which secret sins, services and sorrows are alike inspected.
A watching with two different ends, waiting until one man's iniquity is full and for an opportunity to aid the other.
An examination: men are held so close under the eye that nothing escapes.

outliers.note: Caps his note on the soft answer with a Latin jingle to the same effect, that heavy anger is broken when the reply is sweet.

Turns the second verse into a catalogue of the practical difficulties of speech — when to speak and when to keep silent, what to say and what to omit, and what manner fits the occasion and the persons — concluding that even wise counsel may be foolishly given.

themes: A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.
The tongue of the wise useth knowledge aright: but the mouth of fools poureth out foolishness.
The eyes of the Lord are in every place, beholding the evil and the good.
A wholesome tongue is a tree of life: but perverseness therein is a breach in the spirit.
A fool despiseth his father’s instruction: but he that regardeth reproof is prudent.
In the house of the righteous is much treasure: but in the revenues of the wicked is trouble.
The lips of the wise disperse knowledge: but the heart of the foolish doeth not so.

8.pericope_label: The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the Lord: but the prayer of the upright is his delight... The heart of him that hath understanding seeketh knowledge: but the mouth of fools feedeth on foolishness

schools.summary: Delitzsch explains why sacrifice is assigned to the godless and prayer to the upright, sacrifice being a material and legally required performance nearer to dead works than prayer, which completes itself in a word; he also identifies the syllogism of the eleventh verse as an inference from lesser to greater, reads the contrast of mocker and wise as evidence that scepticism gained ground in Israel from David's time, and rejects both Luther's rendering and an alternative Hebrew reading in the fourteenth verse. Ellicott presses the same point about cost, and derives the name of the underworld from a verb meaning to ask, since it asks for more and is never satisfied.

Gill keeps the religious exercises of a man in a course of sin worthless whatever their form, records an alternative in which the tenth verse says the man has had bad discipline rather than that correction is grievous to him, and turns the eleventh verse to the certainty that God knows where every man's dust lies.

Clarke holds that no quantity of observance substitutes for holiness and asks who counts as upright, answering that the term reaches the man still weary of his sin as well as the man already saved; on the broken spirit he turns physician, holding that every sorrow but that of true repentance works death and that a habit of sighing shortens life. Wesley reduces the eighth verse to a contrast of cost, the most expensive service against the cheapest.

Henry supplies the motive behind a wicked man's sacrifice, that it stops the mouth of conscience and preserves a reputation as a sanctuary shelters a criminal, observes that of all sinners apostates resent reproof worst, and recommends harmless mirth as an ornament to religion while warning against melancholy.

debates.question: What does the tenth verse say about correction?

positions.view: There is a grievous correction awaiting the man who leaves the way, first as discipline and then, if reproof is still hated, as death.
Whoever will not welcome instruction receives it at last against his will as peremptory punishment, and that sharp correction is the death he falls under.
The clause may instead say that the man has had bad discipline, due care never having been taken of him.
The point is conduct rather than construction: apostates resent reproof worst of all sinners.

debates.question: What does the scorner not love?

positions.view: The man who reproves him; the standing contrast of mocker and wise reflects a real growth of scepticism in Israel.
To reprove himself; he will not retire into his own heart and reason there.

outliers.note: Leaves exegesis for physiology on the broken spirit, holding that the indulgence of a disposition to sighing tends to destroy life, since each deep sigh throws off a portion of the vital energy.

Explains why the worthlessness of sacrifice without obedience needed saying: men are apt to assume that whatever costs trouble and expense must please God, even when the loving heart he alone cares for is absent.

themes: The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the Lord: but the prayer of the upright is his delight.
The way of the wicked is an abomination unto the Lord: but he loveth him that followeth after righteousness.
Correction is grievous unto him that forsaketh the way: and he that hateth reproof shall die.
Hell and destruction are before the Lord: how much more then the hearts of the children of men?
A scorner loveth not one that reproveth him: neither will he go unto the wise.
A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken.
The heart of him that hath understanding seeketh knowledge: but the mouth of fools feedeth on foolishness.

15.pericope_label: All the days of the afflicted are evil: but he that is of a merry heart hath a continual feast... Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established

schools.summary: Delitzsch takes the afflicted man for one genuinely pressed whose trouble renews itself each morning, makes the trouble of the sixteenth verse the restless care of a man enslaved to money, rejects an emendation of the slothful into the tyrannical, reads the twentieth verse as the editor's mark of a third main division of the collection, and refuses to let any proverb against much counsel become a rule of morals; Ellicott, by contrast, takes the afflicted for a man who makes the worst of everything, and reads the sluggard's thorns as excuses for inaction.

Gill reads the afflicted as the poor in purse or in knowledge, recovers a Latin dramatist's phrase for the cheap earthy supper of the seventeenth verse, and records a rendering of the last verse in which what is lacking is not counsel but secrecy.

Clarke has the sluggard imagine ten thousand insuperable difficulties, all of them creatures of an imagination formed by his own sloth, notes that contentment follows the fear of God, and suggests that the counsellors of the last verse may be a single chief of council; Wesley itemises the trouble that attends great treasure and glosses the widow's border as the estate lying within it.

Henry turns the afflicted man into an object of duty rather than diagnosis, calls passion the great make-bate and meekness the peace-maker, and describes the wicked man's appetite for folly as a fish taking the bait without dread of the hook.

debates.question: Who is the afflicted man of the fifteenth verse?

positions.view: Not one bearing real misfortune but one who makes the worst of everything; the proverb is a caution against anxiety.
A man genuinely pressed from without or within, for whom each new day renews the feeling of his trouble.
The poor, whether in purse or in knowledge, or the troubled in mind.
Whoever he is, he is to be pitied and relieved rather than diagnosed, since the case might be our own.

debates.question: What is lacking in the last verse?

positions.view: Counsel; the man who scorns to consult is defeated by circumstances a little consultation would have foreseen.
Possibly secrecy: a man who publishes his intentions can expect them frustrated.
The plural of the second line may name a chief of the council rather than a multitude of counsellors.

outliers.note: Reads the proverb about a wise son structurally, noting that the collection opened with a proverb on honouring parents, that a second main division began the same way, and that the editor marks a third division here with a proverb of the same kind.
Recovers from a Latin comic dramatist the phrase for a harsh and earthly supper made of what grows out of the ground, and notes that the Hebrew word for the dish means a traveller's meal.

themes: All the days of the afflicted are evil: but he that is of a merry heart hath a continual feast.
Better is little with the fear of the Lord than great treasure and trouble therewith.
Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith.
A wrathful man stirreth up strife: but he that is slow to anger appeaseth strife.
The way of the slothful man is as an hedge of thorns: but the way of the righteous is made plain.
A wise son maketh a glad father: but a foolish man despiseth his mother.
Folly is joy to him that is destitute of wisdom: but a man of understanding walketh uprightly.
Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established.

23.pericope_label: A man hath joy by the answer of his mouth: and a word spoken in due season, how good is it!... He that is greedy of gain troubleth his own house; but he that hateth gifts shall live

schools.summary: Delitzsch guards the first verse against sounding like praise of self-complacency, the Hebrew meaning a reply that fits what was said; he identifies the widow's landmark as the object of the proud man's encroachment, defends a shortened verb form as elevated style, and notes that from the greedy man onward the Greek version begins mingling these proverbs with those of the next chapter. Ellicott counts a suitable reply a gift of God, infers from repeated legislation that moving a boundary stone was a common oppression, and reverses the English of the twenty-sixth verse so that pleasant words are what is pure in God's sight.

Gill takes the joy of the answer as the pleasure of being useful to a friend, notes the alternative rendering of the wicked man's thoughts as thoughts of evil, and adds to the greedy man's household the servants denied time to eat and sleep.

Clarke finds a threefold antithesis in the upward way — wise against fool, above against below, life against death — observes that proud families are seldom long continued, and describes the covetous man as a torment to himself and a curse to those he deals with; Wesley makes the way of life a matter of where a man places his heart and treasure, and glosses the widow's border as the estate within it.

Henry supplies the practical morals: that many a good word fails for want of being well timed, that God delights to abase the elevated and support the dejected, that thoughts are words to God, and that the covetous man becomes a vexation to his own children and servants.

debates.question: How much does the upward way of life claim?

positions.view: A full antithesis of heaven against hell, above against below, life against death.
Possibly no more than long life on earth and escape from an early death, though the words sound like a faint echo of the apostle's language about a citizenship above.
The way of life is one though it comprises many paths, and the word for upwards is the one used in the book's unresolved question whether a man's spirit rises at death.

debates.question: What does the second half of the twenty-sixth verse say?

positions.view: That pleasant words are pure in God's sight, accepted as coming from a well-meaning heart — not that the words of the pure are pleasant.
The halves are not to be separated at all, since thoughts are words to God and words are judged by the thoughts they come from.
The first clause may be read as thoughts of evil rather than the thoughts of evil men.

outliers.note: Records that from the twenty-seventh verse onward the Greek version begins mingling the proverbs of this chapter with those of the following one.
Explains the joy of a fitting answer by the danger of speech: the tongue does so much mischief and slips so often that a suitable reply may fairly be counted a gift of God.

themes: A man hath joy by the answer of his mouth: and a word spoken in due season, how good is it!
The way of life is above to the wise, that he may depart from hell beneath.
The Lord will destroy the house of the proud: but he will establish the border of the widow.
The thoughts of the wicked are an abomination to the Lord: but the words of the pure are pleasant words.
He that is greedy of gain troubleth his own house; but he that hateth gifts shall live.

28.pericope_label: The heart of the righteous studieth to answer: but the mouth of the wicked poureth out evil things... The fear of the Lord is the instruction of wisdom; and before honour is humility

schools.summary: Delitzsch canvasses what the versions made of the studied answer — faithfulness, obedience, even wormwood — corrects the distance of God from the wicked to a withdrawal of gracious presence rather than of space, challenges an emendation of the light of the eyes, presses the Hebrew for soul as the bond between intellectual and bodily life so that despising it is suicide, and declines to settle whether the fear of the Lord is the subject or the predicate of the last proverb; Ellicott alone reads the light of the eyes as the sight of another person's happiness, and renders the last verse as a discipline leading to wisdom.

Gill distinguishes God's essential presence, which is everywhere, from his favour, which is withdrawn, reads the light of the eyes of the things seen rather than the power of seeing, and qualifies the studied answer by the extraordinary case in which disciples were told not to premeditate a defence.

Clarke says the righteous man's tongue never runs before his wit, turns the light of the eyes into a programme of self-instruction from nature and art, calls the despising of one's own soul constructive rather than actual, and closes the chapter by observing that men who rose from low life to positions of trust have been remarkable for humility, since providence never elevates the proud; Wesley draws the contrast that the wicked man speaks from the mouth and not the heart.

Henry makes the governed tongue the proof of a wise man, supplies the reciprocity by which men who tell God to depart find that he has, explains the reproof of life as both livingly given and life-giving, and identifies the sinner's fundamental error as an undervaluing of his own soul.

debates.question: What is the light of the eyes?

positions.view: The things seen rather than the faculty of sight — gardens, rivers, hills, and above all light itself.
The sight of another person whose eyes are bright with happiness.
An occasion of endless self-instruction from the beauties of nature and art.
A lexical question first: whether the noun can mean brightness at all, or only a lamp.

debates.question: How should the last proverb of the chapter be construed?

positions.view: Undecided: the clause may be predicate, making the fear of God the aim of Wisdom's teaching, or subject, making it the school in which wisdom is learned.
A discipline which leads to wisdom, humility leading likewise to honour.
An awe of God on the spirit which prompts the wisest counsels and chastises unwise words.
The summary of what the book has said of this fear, that it is at once the beginning of wisdom, the beginning of knowledge, and the instruction of wisdom.

outliers.note: Defines the despising of one's own soul in the strongest available terms, the Hebrew word meaning more than the later word for self and naming the bond between the intellectual and the bodily life, so that to neglect it is to expose one's life — in a word, suicide.
Ends the chapter on a claim about providence rather than about the text, that men raised from low life to positions of trust have been remarkable for humility and that a proud man is never elevated.

themes: The heart of the righteous studieth to answer: but the mouth of the wicked poureth out evil things.
The Lord is far from the wicked: but he heareth the prayer of the righteous.
The light of the eyes rejoiceth the heart: and a good report maketh the bones fat.
The ear that heareth the reproof of life abideth among the wise.
He that refuseth instruction despiseth his own soul: but he that heareth reproof getteth understanding.
The fear of the Lord is the instruction of wisdom; and before honour is humility.
